launch-tn-nashville-centennial-park.description: The full-scale Parthenon is Centennial Park's central landmark and a separately ticketed art museum; outdoor views remain free when the museum is closed.
Alan LeQuire's 42-foot Athena statue stands inside the Parthenon museum, so seeing it requires paid admission during museum hours.
Lake Watauga anchors the park loop and provides water views and seasonal wildlife, but it is not a swimming or wading area.
The Sunken Garden is a free formal garden near the Parthenon with seasonal plantings, paths, benches, and frequent portrait activity.
Musicians Corner presents free seasonal concerts and family programming on the park lawn; event dates, vendors, weather rules, and entry points vary.
Centennial Dog Park has separate fenced areas for large and small dogs on Flag Pole Hill and follows dawn-to-dusk hours rather than the full park schedule.
Centennial Art Center offers rotating galleries, classes, and workshops on its own schedule; gallery access is generally free while classes require registration.
Centennial Sportsplex is a separately operated indoor recreation complex with pools, ice rinks, tennis, fitness programs, fees, and its own parking and hours.

launch-tn-nashville-shelby-bottoms-and-s.description: Shelby Bottoms Nature Center is the best first stop for maps, exhibits, staff guidance, restrooms, nature play, and the main paved greenway trailhead.
Cornelia Fort Airpark preserves a former runway as broad paved open space used for walking, cycling, events, and greenway connections away from the Nature Center.
The Cumberland River Pedestrian Bridge carries the greenway across the river toward Two Rivers Park; the exposed span can be hot, windy, or slick.
The main trailhead at the Nature Center begins the accessible paved greenway and connects to primitive floodplain paths, boardwalks, and river overlooks.
Sevier Lake is a quiet Shelby Park destination for views and fishing under posted rules; it is not a supervised swimming area.
Shelby Park's developed play area serves family visits near recreation fields and picnic space, separate from the wilder Shelby Bottoms trail system.
Shelby Golf Course is a separately operated public course with tee times, fees, clubhouse services, and boundaries that are not ordinary park space.
Observation platforms along Shelby Bottoms provide wetland and wildlife views; route conditions and visibility change with flooding, vegetation, and seasonal closures.

launch-tn-nashville-warner-parks.description: Warner Park Nature Center is the best orientation point for maps, exhibits, ranger help, restrooms, nature play, and Edwin Warner trail access.
Mossy Ridge is a strenuous natural-surface loop from the Deep Well area with sustained hills, roots, rocks, mud, and limited facilities.
Harpeth Woods Trail is a shorter forest loop near the Nature Center, but it still includes natural surfaces, grades, roots, and weather-dependent conditions.
The stone steps and tree-lined Allée are a signature Percy Warner landmark reached from the Belle Meade Boulevard entrance; the long stairway has no step-free equivalent.
Luke Lea Heights provides one of the system's broadest overlooks after a hilly approach; haze, foliage, road access, and weather affect the view.
Warner Dog Park is a fenced off-leash destination with its own lot; dogs elsewhere remain leashed and are excluded from posted habitat and equestrian areas.
The designated mountain-bike trail uses one-way natural-surface riding rules and closes when wet enough for tires to damage the route.
The Iroquois Steeplechase grounds are an event and equestrian destination within Percy Warner Park; ordinary access changes around races and private operations.

launch-tn-nashville-bicentennial-capitol.description: The 200-foot Tennessee Map Plaza is a walkable granite map with county, city, river, highway, and railroad details; supervise children around fountain edges.
The Pathway of History traces Tennessee's timeline along the western side of the mall through engraved markers, memorials, and interpretive stops.
Thirty-one vertical fountains represent Tennessee's major waterways and operate seasonally or as maintenance permits; they should not be promised as active without checking.
The 95-bell carillon represents Tennessee's counties and sounds on a programmed schedule near the Capitol-facing end of the park.
The Court of 3 Stars references Tennessee's three grand divisions and forms a ceremonial plaza near the carillon and Capitol view.
The outdoor amphitheater hosts concerts, ceremonies, and public programs; event setup can restrict seating, paths, and nearby parking.
Nashville Farmers Market borders the park with restaurants, shops, produce vendors, and restrooms on schedules separate from the outdoor state park.
The central mall frames a direct uphill view toward the Tennessee State Capitol, with broad paved approaches but little shade in hot weather.

launch-tn-nashville-wasioto-park.description: The Hollow is a sculpted play landscape with climbing, sliding, and imaginative exploration; surfaces can become hot or slick and require close supervision.
The Scoops are distinctive bowl-shaped play elements within the children's landscape, intended for active play under adult supervision.
The Gorge combines climbing nets, steps, and elevated play within the riverfront landscape; use depends on maintenance, weather, and posted restrictions.
Explorer Trail links play and landscape features through the park, offering a shorter family route rather than a long-distance greenway trail.
The seasonal spray ground has required extensive repairs and is currently listed by Metro Parks as closed; verify reopening before planning water play.
The riverfront amphitheater is a reservable performance and gathering space with skyline views; events can change public access and nearby parking.
The Shelby Street Pedestrian Bridge elevator provides step-free access between bridge level and the park when operating, but renovation or outages may require the long ramp approach.
The Lawn is flexible riverfront space for picnics, play, skyline views, and programmed events, with limited shade and event-dependent availability.

launch-tn-nashville-radnor-lake-state-na.description: Walter Criley Visitor Center is the west-side orientation point for maps, staff help, exhibits, programs, restrooms, and current trail and parking conditions.
Lake Trail follows a mostly gentle natural route along the water with wildlife views; roots, mud, narrow sections, and sanctuary rules still apply.
Ganier Ridge is a strenuous forest loop with steep grades, roots, rocks, and elevation change; it is not an accessible lakeside stroll.
South Cove Trail climbs through forest south of the lake and connects to ridge routes, with natural surfaces and no facilities once underway.
Otter Creek Road is reserved for pedestrians through the natural area during normal operation and offers the smoothest extended route beside the lake.
The Barbara J. Mapp Aviary Education Center supports raptor education and programs on a schedule separate from the trails and main visitor center.
East Lake Trail provides quieter natural-surface access from the east side, where parking is limited and trail conditions remain weather dependent.
West-side parking serves the visitor center and major trail connections but fills early on pleasant weekends; illegal shoulder parking is not an overflow plan.

launch-tn-nashville-fort-negley-park.description: The free Visitor Center provides exhibits, films, maps, restrooms, and current construction guidance during shorter Tuesday-through-Saturday hours.
The historic hilltop fort is temporarily closed during phase-one construction in 2026; visitors should not bypass barriers or assume the upper structure is accessible.
The roughly half-mile park walking trail remains the principal outdoor route during construction, with temporary approaches and work-zone boundaries.
Open portions of the elevated landscape provide a broad Nashville skyline view, though construction fencing and vegetation can change the best viewpoint.
Outdoor panels explain Union-occupied Nashville, the African American laborers who built the fort, Civil War history, archaeology, and WPA reconstruction.
The native meadow supports habitat around the historic landscape and should be viewed from maintained routes rather than entered or picked.
The Chestnut Street approach is affected by the current construction plan; follow temporary wayfinding rather than relying on an older map or entrance memory.
The memorial landscape connects the site's military history with the lives and labor of the people who built it; use the interpretation to understand more than the remaining stonework.

launch-tn-nashville-two-rivers-park.description: Wave Country is a separately ticketed seasonal aquatic center with wave pool, slides, supervision rules, capacity limits, and weather-dependent operation.
Two Rivers Golf Course is a separately operated public course with fees, tee times, clubhouse services, and boundaries that are not ordinary park space.
Two Rivers Mansion is a historic house museum and event destination with tours and interior access on a schedule separate from the surrounding park.
Two Rivers Skatepark is a free concrete riding area for skateboards, scooters, and similar wheeled use under posted safety and conduct rules.
The disc-golf course crosses a distinct recreation zone; watch for flying discs, follow course flow, and avoid using fairways as picnic space.
Two Rivers Dog Park is a fenced off-leash destination with its own access area; leash dogs outside the enclosure and follow posted gate rules.
The Cumberland River Pedestrian Bridge links Two Rivers with Shelby Bottoms and the regional greenway network across an exposed, unsheltered span.
The Stones River Greenway trailhead begins paved river and neighborhood connections; choose this arrival point for trail travel rather than the mansion or aquatic center.
